sydney-opera-house.blurb: The sails are covered in more than a million Swedish-made tiles that clean themselves when it rains. Utzon's winning entry in the 1957 competition was little more than a set of sketches, and working out how to build the shells took years: the answer was to cut them all from the surface of one imaginary sphere. As costs and delays mounted, Utzon resigned in 1966 and left Australia, never to return. A local team finished the building, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1973. Today it hosts more than 1,800 performances a year.

eiffel-tower.blurb: Gustave Eiffel's company built it for the 1889 World's Fair, with a permit for just 20 years. Leading Parisian artists signed a protest against this 'useless and monstrous' tower before it went up. At 300 m (330 m today, with its antennas) it was the tallest structure in the world until New York's Chrysler Building passed it in 1930. Around 2.5 million rivets hold its wrought iron together, and it is repainted by hand roughly every seven years. On hot days the metal expands and the tower grows by up to about 15 cm.

burj-khalifa.blurb: At 828 m it's so tall that you can watch the sun set from the ground, ride the lift up and watch it set again. Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it has been the world's tallest building since it opened in 2010. Its Y-shaped floor plan, inspired by a desert flower, steps back as it climbs, which breaks up the wind. The spire alone, about 240 m, is taller than many skyscrapers. Some of its structural steel was salvaged from the demolished Palace of the Republic in East Berlin.

colosseum.blurb: Begun under Emperor Vespasian in AD 72 and finished under his son Titus in 80, it is the largest amphitheatre ever built. Crowds of some 50,000 to 80,000 came for gladiator fights, animal hunts, executions and re-enacted battles. Under the arena floor ran a maze of tunnels and lifts that hoisted animals and scenery up through trapdoors, and a huge awning worked by sailors could shade the seats. After Rome fell it served as a quarry, a fortress, workshops and even housing, which is why so much of it is missing.

taj-mahal.blurb: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned it in 1631 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child; he was later buried beside her. Some 20,000 workers are said to have spent over two decades on the complex. The white marble is inlaid with semi-precious stones, while the mosque and guest house on either side are of red sandstone. Everything is mirrored around one axis except Shah Jahan's own tomb, added later. The marble seems to change colour through the day, from pinkish at dawn to milky white at noon.

empire-state-building.blurb: Designed by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon, it went up in just over a year, at times rising about four and a half storeys a week. It opened in 1931 as the world's tallest building and kept the title for nearly 40 years, until the World Trade Center's North Tower passed it in 1970. Its mast was first meant as a mooring post for airships, an idea quickly dropped as too dangerous. The building has its own ZIP code, and lightning strikes it about 20 times a year.

sagrada-familia.blurb: Construction began in 1882, and Antoni Gaudí took over a year later, devoting the rest of his life to it. When he died in 1926 less than a quarter was finished, and he is buried in its crypt. Asked why it was taking so long, he reportedly replied that his client was not in a hurry. Paid for only by donations, it has risen slowly ever since; in 1936 anarchists set fire to the crypt and destroyed many of his plans. Inside, the columns branch like trees into a stone forest, lit by coloured glass. It is now the tallest church in the world.

st-basils.blurb: Ivan the Terrible ordered it in 1555 to celebrate the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan. It is really several churches in one: eight chapels around a central one, each with its own dome, and a tenth chapel was added in 1588 over the grave of the holy fool Vasily, who gave the cathedral its popular name. Legend says Ivan blinded the architects so they could never build anything as beautiful again, which is almost certainly untrue. The famous bright colours came later; it was completed with them in 1683.

petronas-towers.blurb: From 1998 to 2004 these 88-storey towers were the tallest buildings in the world, and they are still the tallest twin towers. Architect César Pelli based their floor plan on an eight-pointed Islamic star. A two-storey skybridge links them at the 41st and 42nd floors. It isn't fixed rigidly to the towers, so it can slide as they sway in the wind. The towers were built by two rival teams, one led by a Japanese firm and one by a Korean firm, which turned construction into a race.

leaning-tower-pisa.blurb: It is the bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, and it began to lean during construction in the 12th century because the soft ground couldn't carry its weight. Work stopped for almost a century, partly because of wars, which gave the soil time to settle and probably saved it from collapse. The builders then made the upper floors slightly taller on one side to compensate, so the tower is actually a little curved. By 1990 it leaned 5.5 degrees; engineers spent the next decade removing soil from under the high side, bringing it back to just under 4.

parthenon.blurb: Built between 447 and 438 BC, the temple was dedicated to Athena and also served as Athens' treasury. Its columns lean slightly inwards and its floor rises gently in the middle, subtle corrections that make it look perfectly straight from a distance. Over the centuries it became a church and then a mosque. It stood largely intact until 1687, when a Venetian shell hit gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside. Many of its surviving sculptures were taken to Britain by Lord Elgin in the early 1800s and are still in the British Museum.

big-ben.blurb: Big Ben is strictly the name of the great bell, but everyone uses it for the tower too, officially the Elizabeth Tower since 2012. Designed by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin and finished in 1859, it rises 96 m, with 334 steps up to the belfry. The first great bell cracked during testing, and its replacement cracked soon after it was hung, so it still rings slightly out of tune. The clock is famously reliable: old pennies placed on the pendulum fine-tune it, each one changing its speed by about two-fifths of a second a day.

forbidden-city.blurb: Built between 1406 and 1420, it was home to 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties for almost 500 years, and ordinary people were not allowed in. Legend says it has 9,999 rooms, one short of the 10,000 of heaven; a survey counted 8,886. Its yellow roof tiles were a colour reserved for the emperor. The last emperor, Puyi, left in 1924, and since 1925 it has been the Palace Museum. It is the largest surviving palace complex in the world, and now one of the most visited places on Earth.

notre-dame.blurb: Building began in 1163 and was largely finished by 1260. Its flying buttresses, rib vaults and huge rose windows made it one of the great works of French Gothic. During the French Revolution much of its religious imagery was smashed. Victor Hugo's 1831 novel about its hunchbacked bell-ringer made it famous again and helped save it from ruin, leading to a major restoration in the 1800s that added the spire. That spire collapsed in the fire of April 2019, and after five years of rebuilding the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

pantheon.blurb: The building you see was completed by Emperor Hadrian around AD 126, but the inscription on the front still names Agrippa, who built an earlier temple on the site. Almost 2,000 years later its dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. The concrete gets lighter towards the top, with volcanic pumice mixed in, and the coffers in the ceiling cut the weight further. It has been a church since 609. When it rains, water falls through the open eye at the top, about 8 m across, and drains away through small holes in the floor.

cn-tower.blurb: Built by the railway company Canadian National, hence the name, it was finished in 1976 to send TV and radio signals over Toronto's growing skyline. At 553 m it was the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years, until the Burj Khalifa passed it. It has a glass floor 342 m up and a revolving restaurant at about 350 m. Thrill-seekers can walk around the outside of the main pod on the EdgeWalk, strapped to a rail 356 m above the ground. It is struck by lightning dozens of times a year.

hagia-sophia.blurb: Emperor Justinian had it built in just five years, finishing in 537, after riots had destroyed the church before it. For nearly a thousand years it was the largest cathedral in the world, and its huge dome resting on pendentives changed the history of architecture. The first dome collapsed after an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt taller. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453 it became a mosque and gained its minarets. It was a museum from 1935 and became a mosque again in 2020; its Byzantine mosaics are still there, some covered during prayers.

marina-bay-sands.blurb: Designed by Moshe Safdie and opened in 2010, the resort cost about S$8 billion, then the most expensive casino property in the world. Its three 55-storey hotel towers are topped by the SkyPark, a 340 m platform that looks like a ship balanced on the roofs. The rooftop pool is about 150 m long and sits some 200 m above the bay. The deck overhangs the north tower by about 67 m, the largest public cantilevered platform in the world. Down by the water there is even a floating Apple store.

guggenheim-bilbao.blurb: When Frank Gehry's museum opened in 1997, it turned a declining industrial port into a destination, a boost now known as the 'Bilbao effect'. Its curves were designed with CATIA, software made for designing fighter jets. The titanium skin, less than half a millimetre thick, ripples like fish scales and changes colour with the weather. Outside, Jeff Koons's giant Puppy, covered in flowers, guards the entrance, and Louise Bourgeois's huge spider sculpture stands by the river.

neuschwanstein.blurb: King Ludwig II of Bavaria began it in 1869 as a private retreat, inspired by medieval legends and the operas of his hero Richard Wagner. Behind the fairy-tale towers it had modern comforts such as central heating, running water and telephone lines. He paid for it from his own fortune, not the state's, but ran up huge debts. Ludwig lived there only a few months before he was deposed and died mysteriously in 1886. It opened to paying visitors weeks later, and it inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.

fallingwater.blurb: Frank Lloyd Wright designed it in the mid-1930s as a weekend house for the Pittsburgh department store owner Edgar Kaufmann and his wife Liliane. The family expected a house with a view of their favourite waterfall; Wright put them right on top of it, so you hear the water throughout the house. Its concrete terraces reach out over the stream, anchored to the rock. They began to sag almost at once and kept sagging for decades, until engineers reinforced them with steel cables in 2002. It has been open to visitors since 1964.

villa-savoye.blurb: Le Corbusier and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret built this weekend house for the Savoye family between 1928 and 1931. It shows his 'five points' of modern architecture: pillars that lift it off the ground, a roof garden, a free plan, long strip windows and a free facade. A ramp leads you up through the house, and the curve of the ground floor followed the turning circle of a car. The roof leaked so badly that the family complained for years, and the house was later nearly demolished. Today it is a protected monument and one of the most influential houses of the 20th century.

chrysler-building.blurb: Walter Chrysler paid for it himself as an investment for his children; it was never his company's headquarters. It was racing 40 Wall Street to be the world's tallest building, so the builders secretly assembled its 38 m spire inside the crown and raised it into place in about 90 minutes. It held the title for less than a year before the Empire State Building passed it. Its gargoyles are steel eagle heads and radiator caps modelled on Chrysler cars, and its crown is clad in gleaming stainless steel.

lotus-temple.blurb: Designed by the Iranian-born architect Fariborz Sahba and dedicated in 1986, it is a Bahá'í House of Worship, open to people of every faith. Its 27 marble-clad concrete petals stand in three rings of nine, like a half-open lotus. There is no altar, no clergy and no sermons, yet it draws several million visitors a year. Nine pools surround the building, completing the lotus and helping keep the hall cool. On its completion it was compared with the Sydney Opera House, and it has won awards from engineering bodies around the world.

sheikh-zayed-mosque.blurb: Built between 1994 and 2007, it is the largest mosque in the United Arab Emirates and was the idea of the country's founding president, Sheikh Zayed, who is buried in its courtyard. It blends styles from across the Islamic world, with 82 white domes and four minarets. The carpet in the main prayer hall, hand-knotted by about 1,200 artisans, is one of the largest in the world, and the main chandelier is one of the largest too. Reflecting pools line the arcades, whose white marble columns are inlaid with flowers in semi-precious stones.

atomium.blurb: Built as the centrepiece of the 1958 World's Fair in Brussels, it shows the unit cell of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times. It was meant to stand for just six months and never came down. Its nine steel spheres, each 18 m across, are linked by tubes holding stairs, escalators and what was then the fastest lift in Europe. Six spheres can be visited, and the top one holds a restaurant with a view over all of Brussels. A renovation in 2004 to 2006 replaced its original aluminium skin with stainless steel.

alhambra.blurb: Its name means 'the red one', after the colour of its walls. Begun in 1238 on a hill above Granada, it was the palace and fortress of the Nasrid rulers, the last Muslim dynasty in Spain, and most of its famous halls date from the 14th century. Inside, walls and ceilings are covered in carved stucco, tiles and Arabic poetry, and water runs through courtyards such as the Court of the Lions. After 1492 it became a royal court of Ferdinand and Isabella, where Columbus won backing for his voyage.

potala-palace.blurb: From 1649 until 1959 it was the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas. The 5th Dalai Lama began the present building in 1645 on a hill in the middle of the Lhasa valley, about 3,700 m above sea level, so many visitors are out of breath before they reach the top. It rises 13 storeys and holds more than 1,000 rooms. Its sloping stone walls are up to 5 m thick at the base, and copper was poured into the foundations to protect it from earthquakes. The White Palace held living quarters and offices; the Red Palace is devoted to prayer and holds the tombs of past Dalai Lamas.

angkor-wat.blurb: The Khmer king Suryavarman II built it in the early 12th century as a Hindu temple to Vishnu; it later became Buddhist and still is today. It is the largest religious monument in the world. Its five lotus-bud towers stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, and the wide moat for the oceans around it. Unlike most temples at Angkor, it faces west. Its sandstone blocks came from quarries tens of kilometres away, probably by canal. Its galleries carry hundreds of metres of carved reliefs, and it is the centrepiece of Cambodia's national flag.

cctv-hq.blurb: Designed by Rem Koolhaas and Ole Scheeren of OMA, it is the headquarters of China's state broadcaster. Rather than reaching straight up, its two leaning towers join at the top and bottom to form a skewed loop. The overhanging corner juts out about 75 m in mid-air, and the two halves were joined early one morning, when the steel on both sides was at the same temperature. The irregular grid on its facade is densest where the structure works hardest. Locals nicknamed it 'big pants'.

oslo-opera-house.blurb: Designed by the Norwegian firm Snøhetta and opened in 2008, it is home to the national opera and ballet. Its white roof slopes down into the fjord, so you can walk straight up onto it, and locals picnic, sunbathe and skateboard there. The angled surfaces are clad in white granite and Carrara marble from Italy, so the building seems to rise out of the water. The main auditorium, lined with oak, seats about 1,360. It is the largest cultural building in Norway since Nidaros Cathedral was finished around 1300.

elbphilharmonie.blurb: Designed by Herzog & de Meuron, Hamburg's concert hall sits on top of an old brick warehouse from 1963, its glass crown shaped like a wave or a sail. A curved escalator 82 m long carries you up through the warehouse to a public plaza with views over the harbour. The main hall is lined with about 10,000 gypsum panels, each with its own pattern of dimples to spread the sound. Costs grew to about ten times the original budget and it opened years late, in 2017, but Hamburg got a world-class concert hall.

brasilia-cathedral.blurb: Oscar Niemeyer designed it for Brazil's brand-new capital, and it was dedicated in 1970. Sixteen curved concrete columns, each weighing about 90 tonnes, rise like hands reaching to the sky and hold up a crown of glass. Most of the church sits below ground: you enter through a dark passage and emerge into a bright hall full of coloured light. Angels hang from the ceiling on steel cables, and four bronze evangelists guard the entrance.

taipei-101.blurb: With 101 floors above ground, it was the world's tallest building from 2004 until the Burj Khalifa in 2009. Its design echoes a stalk of bamboo, rising in eight sections of eight floors, eight being a lucky number in Chinese culture. Near the top hangs a 660-tonne steel ball that sways to steady the tower in typhoons and earthquakes; it is so popular that it has its own cartoon mascots, the 'Damper Babies'. Its lifts were once the fastest in the world, climbing from the 5th to the 89th floor in 37 seconds.

habitat-67.blurb: Moshe Safdie developed it from his university thesis and built it in his twenties for the Expo 67 world's fair in Montreal. It is made of 354 identical concrete boxes, cast on site and stacked by crane into a hilly village of apartments. Safdie wanted to give city dwellers a garden, so each unit's terrace is the roof of the one below. It was meant as a prototype for affordable housing, but its flats became sought after instead. Safdie still keeps an apartment there.

kunsthaus-graz.blurb: Designed by Peter Cook and Colin Fournier, it opened in 2003, when Graz was European Capital of Culture, and shows contemporary art. The blue acrylic blob, with nozzle-shaped skylights pointing north, sits among the red roofs of the old town like a creature that has just landed. Locals call it 'the friendly alien', and the nickname stuck so well that the museum uses it too. At night its skin becomes a giant low-resolution screen made of 930 fluorescent rings, showing images and messages across the river.

heydar-aliyev-center.blurb: Zaha Hadid's cultural centre in Baku opened in 2012 and holds a museum, a concert hall and galleries. There are almost no straight lines anywhere: the building rises from the landscape in one continuous white wave. Its skin is made of thousands of panels, nearly every one a different shape. Inside, floors flow into walls and ceilings without a break. In 2014 it won the Design of the Year award from London's Design Museum.

jatiya-sangsad.blurb: Louis Kahn designed it in the 1960s for what was then East Pakistan, and building work stopped during Bangladesh's 1971 war of independence. It was finished in 1982, eight years after Kahn's death, as the parliament of the new country. The complex covers more than 200 acres, one of the largest legislative complexes in the world. Huge circles, triangles and rectangles cut into its concrete walls let light in while shading the rooms from the sun. Surrounded by an artificial lake, the parliament seems to float.

great-mosque-djenne.blurb: It is the largest mud-brick building in the world. A mosque has stood here since around the 13th century, but the current one dates from 1907. Every year the rains wear away its walls, so the whole town joins a festival to replaster it with fresh mud. The palm-wood sticks poking out of the walls are built-in scaffolding for the job, and they also help the walls cope with changes in temperature. Its great facade faces the market square, and the old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

hallgrimskirkja.blurb: Named after the 17th-century poet and pastor Hallgrímur Pétursson, it is the largest church in Iceland. Architect Guðjón Samúelsson designed it in 1937, and it took 41 years to build, finally finishing in 1986. Its stepped concrete wings are said to recall the basalt columns that form when lava cools. At about 75 m it is one of the tallest structures in Iceland, and a lift takes you up the tower for a view over Reykjavík. A statue of the explorer Leif Erikson, a gift from the USA, stands outside.

niteroi-mac.blurb: Oscar Niemeyer designed this contemporary art museum, finished in 1996, on a cliff across the bay from Rio de Janeiro. A single central column holds up the whole saucer, which is often compared to a UFO, and Niemeyer described it rising from its reflecting pool like a flower. A curving red ramp leads visitors up to the entrance. Inside, a ring of windows around the gallery frames Guanabara Bay, Rio and Sugarloaf Mountain.

lalibela-st-george.blurb: It is one of eleven churches cut straight down into the rock at Lalibela, named after King Lalibela, who commissioned them around 1200. Seen from above, it is a cross carved from a single block of volcanic rock, standing in a pit about 12 m deep. Nothing was built up: everything, from the roof to the windows, was carved down and hollowed out. Legend says angels helped with the work by night. It is still a working church and a place of pilgrimage for Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.

jewish-museum-berlin.blurb: Daniel Libeskind's zinc-clad zigzag, opened in 2001, holds the largest Jewish museum in Europe, telling the history of Jews in Germany. The building has no entrance of its own: you go in through the Baroque building next door and down underground. Inside, empty spaces called voids cut through the zigzag; most can be seen but not entered. In the Memory Void you walk over thousands of steel faces by the artist Menashe Kadishman. More than eleven million people visited in its first 16 years.

turning-torso.blurb: Santiago Calatrava designed this 190 m apartment tower in Malmö, opened in 2005, from his sculpture of a twisting human body. It is built from nine cubes of five floors each, every one turned a little further than the one below, so the top floor is a full quarter turn from the bottom. When it opened it was the tallest building in Scandinavia, and it kept the Nordic record until 2022. It holds 147 apartments, and on clear days you can see across the strait to Copenhagen.

bosco-verticale.blurb: Designed by Stefano Boeri's studio and finished in 2014, these two towers in Milan carry hundreds of trees and thousands of shrubs and plants on their balconies, more than 90 species in all. The greenery filters dust, absorbs CO2, shades the flats and attracts birds and insects. Before planting, the trees were grown in a nursery and tested in wind tunnels. Arborists abseil down the facades to prune them. In 2015 it was named the most beautiful and innovative skyscraper in the world.

shwedagon-pagoda.blurb: Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist site, the gilded stupa rises 112 m on a hill above Yangon and is believed to hold relics of four Buddhas, including eight hairs of Gautama Buddha. Tradition says it is more than 2,500 years old; historians date it to between the 6th and 10th centuries. Its outer layer is real gold, and its tip is set with thousands of diamonds and rubies, crowned by a single 76-carat diamond. City rules cap building heights so that it always dominates the skyline.

hassan-ii-mosque.blurb: Completed in 1993 to designs by Michel Pinseau, it stands on a promontory over the Atlantic in Casablanca, and worshippers can pray above the sea. Its minaret is 210 m tall, one of the tallest in the world, and a laser at the top points towards Mecca. It holds about 25,000 worshippers inside and 80,000 more on the esplanade. Some 3,300 Moroccan craftsmen worked on its carved wood, plaster and zellige tilework, and the roof of the prayer hall slides open.

zeitz-mocaa.blurb: This Cape Town museum opened in 2017 inside a grain silo from 1921 that was once the tallest building in sub-Saharan Africa. Thomas Heatherwick's studio carved its atrium out of the silo's 42 concrete tubes in the shape of a single grain of corn, enlarged to fill the space. It is the largest museum of contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora. The pillow-shaped windows of the upper floors bulge outwards and glow like lanterns at night.

cardboard-cathedral.blurb: After the 2011 earthquake badly damaged Christchurch's cathedral, the Japanese architect Shigeru Ban designed this temporary replacement, which opened in 2013. Its A-frame is made of about 90 large cardboard tubes resting on shipping containers. The cardboard is coated with waterproof polyurethane and fire retardant, and a polycarbonate roof keeps out the rain. Built as a stopgap, it was designed to last about 50 years. The triangular stained-glass window at the front reuses images from the old cathedral's rose window.

yoyogi-gymnasium.blurb: Kenzo Tange designed it for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, where it hosted swimming and diving; at the 2020 Games it held handball. Its sweeping roof hangs from two thick steel cables slung between concrete masts, like a suspension bridge, leaving a huge space inside without a single column. The curving shapes also recall the roofs of traditional Japanese temples. It is one of the best-known works of modern Japanese architecture, and Tange went on to win the Pritzker Prize in 1987.
